lesson.title: Reflexive Daily Routines
lesson.subtitle: sich anziehen, aufwachen, einschlafen — the morning round where prefixes and reflexives meet

hook.title: The Morning Is Reflexive
hook.content: Run the tape of your morning in German and watch two systems you already own click together. Ich wache auf (prefix flies). Ich stehe auf (prefix flies). Then the mirror moment: Ich ziehe mich an — I pull myself on. Get dressed takes a REFLEXIVE object in German: you are the thing being dressed. English hides this (I get dressed — dressed by whom?), but the old English would not have: 'I dress me', said without blinking. Add Ich wasche mich and Ich fühle mich gut and the whole morning runs on actions that turn back on their doer.

footnotes.title: zieht ... an: the Prefix Waits, the Pronoun Doesn't
footnotes.content: anziehen is separable (topic 15): the prefix an flies to the end and the reflexive pronoun sits right after the verb — Ich ziehe MICH an. Not mich anziehe, not anziehe mich. Verb, object, prefix: the bracket closes around the pronoun.

pattern.title: The Routine Chain
pattern.content: The full chain, verbs you can already conjugate: Ich wache auf (I wake up). Ich stehe auf (I get up). Ich wasche mich (I wash myself). Ich ziehe mich an (I get dressed). Ich fühle mich gut (I feel good). Ich sehe gut aus (I look good — aussehen, no reflexive needed: the looking goes outward!). Ich freue mich (I am glad). Und abends: Ich schlafe ein (I fall asleep — ein- into sleep). Two honest exceptions inside the routine: aussehen and aufwachen are NOT reflexive in German — the prefix does the work, no pronoun. Wir treffen uns um acht (we meet at eight) — reciprocal sich: each meets the other.
pattern.linguist_note: anziehen: an (on) + ziehen (pull — the tow/tug family). 'To pull on' clothes is the same image English uses, and German makes the puller and the pulled one person: sich anziehen. English 'dress' once meant the same — 'arise and dress yourself' — before the reflexive faded.

exercises.prompt: The routine chain — match each verb phrase with its reading (the last one in dictionary dress):
exercises.target_answer: Ich ziehe mich an, Ich wache auf, Ich stehe auf, Ich schlafe ein, sich ausziehen
exercises.meaning: I get dressed, I wake up, I get up, I fall asleep, to get undressed
exercises.explanation: The chain runs an → auf → ein — and ausziehen closes the day, an's twin in reverse. The schedule around it: die Kurse beginnen um neun, wir bezahlen den Kaffee — factory verbs, no mirror. Three separable prefixes and one reflexive — the morning round mixes both systems you own.

exercises.prompt: Word order with the bracket: which sentence is correct for 'I am getting dressed'?
exercises.meaning: Ich ziehe mich an = I get dressed
exercises.explanation: Verb in position 2, reflexive pronoun right after it, prefix an closes the bracket: ziehe ... mich ... an.

exercises.prompt: Reciprocal sich: 'Wir treffen _____ um acht.' (We meet at eight):
exercises.meaning: Wir treffen uns = we meet (each other)
exercises.explanation: wir → uns: the same reflexive pronoun does reciprocal duty — I meet you, you meet me, one pronoun reports it.

exercises.prompt: Which fossil English phrase still uses the reflexive 'yourself' the way German's sich system does?
exercises.meaning: help yourself — the reflexive imperative English kept
exercises.explanation: Hilf dir! / Help yourself — both languages once reflexive everywhere; English kept the fossil only in set phrases.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the morning, in order: 'I wake up and get dressed'
exercises.target_answer: Ich wache auf und ziehe mich an
exercises.meaning: Ich wache auf und ziehe mich an = I wake up and get dressed

vocab_hints.note: the prefix of aufwachen and aufstehen, flying to the end

exercises.explanation: Two clauses, two flying prefixes — and the second clause tucks its reflexive mich inside the bracket: ziehe mich an.

summary.outcome: Narrate a daily routine mixing separable prefixes and reflexive pronouns, and spot the two non-reflexive exceptions.

use_example.german: Ich wache auf, wasche mich, ziehe mich an und fühle mich gut.
use_example.english: I wake up, wash myself, get dressed and feel good.

summary.takeaway: Routine verbs lean reflexive (sich anziehen, sich fühlen) — but aussehen and aufwachen let the prefix work alone.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: numbers, time & gestern — counting is a shift spiral: drei↔three, zwanzig↔twenty, gestern↔yesterday.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — build in German: "We put on / get dressed (an + ziehen) here today"
twist.explanation: Building "Wir anziehen heute hier" from the lesson's core pattern locks in Reflexive Daily Routines.

anziehen.english_cognate: to put on / get dressed (an + ziehen)
anziehen.english_meaning: to put on / get dressed (an + ziehen)
anziehen.etymology_derivation: Separable: an ('on') + ziehen ('pull' — the tow/tug family, already known): to pull on. Reflexive sich anziehen = get dressed. [wiktionary]

aufwachen.etymology_derivation: Separable: auf (up) + wachen (to be awake/watch); wachen and wake are one verb — a shepherd 'wacht' the flock. [wiktionary]

freuen.etymology_derivation: froh (glad) + -en — froh from Old High German frō, Proto-Germanic *frawaz 'quick, glad'; the English relative is frolic, borrowed from Dutch vrolijk 'joy-ly'. Reflexive: sich freuen. [wiktionary]

ausziehen.english_cognate: to take off, to move out
ausziehen.english_meaning: to take off, to move out
ausziehen.context_phrase: Zuhause ziehe ich die Schuhe aus.
ausziehen.context_translation: At home I take off my shoes.
ausziehen.etymology_derivation: aus (out) + ziehen (to pull): aus is the t-to-s twin of English out, and the root is the *teuhaną of English tug. [wiktionary]

beginnen.context_phrase: Der Film beginnt um acht Uhr.
beginnen.context_translation: The film begins at eight o'clock.
beginnen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *biginnaną; the page documents cognate English begin — an exact class 3 ablaut twin: began and begann, begun and begonnen. [wiktionary]

bezahlen.etymology_derivation: be- + zahlen — the inseparable prefix at work on the tale-family verb. [wiktionary]

brille.etymology_derivation: From Latin beryllus 'beryl' — the gemstone lenses were first made of; no standard English cognate. [wiktionary]

waffel.context_phrase: Ich esse die Waffel mit Marmelade.
waffel.context_translation: I eat the waffle with jam.
waffel.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Middle Dutch wafel; English waffle and wafer come from the same Dutch and Germanic word. [wiktionary]

fremd.context_translation: The city was strange to me.
fremd.etymology_derivation: From Old High German fremidi, Proto-West Germanic *framiþī; English once had the identical word fremd, meaning foreign or strange, now obsolete, and Dutch keeps vreemd. [wiktionary]

jeans.context_phrase: Ich trage heute meine blaue Jeans.
jeans.context_translation: I am wearing my blue jeans today.
jeans.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from English jeans (denim trousers) - a straight English loan. [wiktionary]

mehrere.etymology_derivation: Mehrere is mehr (more — the exact twin of English more) plus -ere; a German-internal formation meaning several. [wiktionary]

firma.context_phrase: Er arbeitet bei einer großen Firma.
firma.context_translation: He works for a big company.
firma.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian firma, a signature from Latin firmare, to make firm — the page lists English firm as cognate. [wiktionary]

schild.context_phrase: Das Schild zeigt den Weg zum Bahnhof.
schild.context_translation: The sign shows the way to the station.
schild.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *skelduz; the page documents cognate English shield — das Schild is the street sign, der Schild the shield. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
